seasons.review_body: Delicious in Dungeon aired January-June 2024 on Netflix and became one of the most critically acclaimed anime releases of the year. Studio Trigger's 24-episode adaptation achieved 100 percent on Rotten Tomatoes across 7 critic reviews and 93 percent with audiences. IGN called it unmissable appointment viewing for its world-building and earnest treatment of food as cultural and emotional subject matter. The premise - cook and eat dungeon monsters - functions as a delivery mechanism for both dungeon-crawling adventure and genuinely inventive worldbuilding, with each creature prepared according to in-universe culinary logic. The show received 16 Crunchyroll Anime Award nominations in 2025 - a record for nominations - but won none, which several outlets attributed to its Netflix exclusivity in a Crunchyroll-dominated awards ecosystem.

episode_reviews.title: Hot Pot / Tart
episode_reviews.review_body:
# Delicious In Dungeon S01E01: "Hot Pot / Tart" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

**Falin** is inside a dragon. Her rescue spell cannot reach her there. The party has been teleported out without its inventory, the map has already wasted a day, and two members have quit because better offers exist elsewhere. That is the premiere's clean trick: it turns fantasy adventure into a bill that has come due. The monster is dangerous, yes, but the first enemy is shortage. Food, money, bodies, time. "Hot Pot / Tart" makes hunger the plot engine, and its best joke is that the joke is also the only workable plan.

## A Rescue Mission With Empty Pockets

The opening sketches a fallen kingdom and a dungeon full of promise, then drags the premise down from myth into logistics. A wrong map has cost the party a day before the run even begins. That detail matters because the clock is already moving. Falin has been eaten, and the failed reach of her spell inside the dragon's stomach gives the rescue mission a hard boundary. This quest has digestion, distance, and delay built into it.

The premiere then tightens the screw with practical humiliation. The teleport that saves the party also strips away their inventory. Survival becomes less about courage than supply. **Chilchuck** adding that two party members have resigned because they received offers elsewhere is funny in the driest way, because the fantasy party collapses like a workplace losing staff to better pay.

That is the episode's smartest register. It refuses to treat heroic urgency as protection from ordinary problems. No gear. No food. Fewer hands. No spare time. The party can want the grand rescue all it likes. The hour keeps asking how they will pay for lunch.

The result is a rescue setup with pressure under every joke. The dragon is still the obvious threat, but the episode makes the road to that dragon feel hostile before anyone draws a weapon. Even getting back into the dungeon requires a plan, and the plan has to work on an empty stomach.

## Laios Makes Hunger The Mission Brief

The tavern conversation is where the premiere locks its premise. The party debates where to eat, and the praised option is comfortingly ordinary: soup with meat dumplings. In another adventure, that would be a pause before the expedition. Here, it becomes the thing they cannot afford.

**Laios** insisting that they will get all their food from the dungeon gives the episode its bite. It sounds ridiculous for about half a second, then brutally logical. If the inventory is gone, money is short, and Falin's rescue cannot wait, the dungeon stops being a place they merely enter. It becomes the supply line.

The writing earns the absurdity by making the argument practical before it becomes cute. The question is not whether monster cuisine sounds appetising. The question is what remains when every normal option has been removed. That is why the food premise lands cleaner than a gag pasted onto a quest. Laios is not derailing the rescue with eccentric hunger. He is translating the rescue into terms the party can survive.

The scene also clarifies Laios without overcomplicating him. His fascination with monsters is strange, and the episode lets the others react to that strangeness. Yet his idea comes from necessity, not whim. That tension gives the character room. He can be alarming at the table and right about the math.

The weakness is that the hour leans heavily on debate to push this turn across. The rapid exchanges keep the energy high, but the argument sometimes states the dilemma instead of sharpening it. Still, the core idea carries the chatter. Desperation has become a recipe.

## The Scorpion Draws The Line

The scorpion beat is the premiere's first real test of its concept. Finding a monster is one thing. Deciding it is gross is easy. Figuring out whether it is safe to eat is where the show starts building its dungeon logic.

That argument matters because it keeps the premise from sliding into random gross-out comedy. The group is eating monsters under pressure, but the episode treats that pressure as a system. They have to negotiate safety, disgust, and knowledge. The scorpion is a body in front of them, and it is a question: can this world be understood well enough to live off it?

This is where **Senshi** matters as more than a new face. The party meets him before moving forward to the second floor, and his arrival changes the monster-food idea from Laios's desperate pitch into a method. The episode needs that pivot. Without someone who treats the dungeon's ecosystem as usable knowledge, the plan risks feeling like a dare performed in armour.

Senshi also gives the food scenes a useful authority. He does not make the concept less strange. He makes it actionable. That distinction matters. The comedy still comes from revulsion and social discomfort, but the cooking has procedure behind it: what to cut, what to avoid, what can become a meal. The dungeon starts to look less like a backdrop and more like an environment with rules.

The scorpion scene has a little first-episode stiffness. The revulsion, safety concern, and necessity land in a fairly direct line. The beat works best as foundation. It tells the viewer what kind of show this is going to be: one where cooking is survival math, and survival math may still look disgusting.

## The Graveyard Plant Is The Better Joke

The plant-based dish resistance gives the episode a sharper comic edge than the scorpion because it finds a contradiction that feels human. The objection is not simple squeamishness. There is a line around what feels inappropriate, especially when plants come from a graveyard. That is funnier and more specific than recoil at monster meat.

The eventual acceptance of the cooked plant dish gives the hour its cleanest little reversal. The same person who resists the idea still continues with the meal after the objections. That does not erase the disgust. It proves the premise. Hunger does not solve the moral unease, but it can sit beside it at the same table.

The joke works because the episode understands that appetite is not a clean moral switch. These characters do not suddenly become fearless dungeon gourmets. They are still broke, still worried, still embarrassed by what survival asks of them. The food can be useful and unsettling in the same bite. That is a better comic engine than shock value, because the laugh comes from watching practical need grind against personal limits.

By the time **Marcille**'s group moves forward to the second floor, the episode has done the necessary first-step work. It has taken a party weakened by loss, resignation, wrong planning, and empty supplies, then handed them a survival system that is comic without being weightless. The title's split between hot pot and tart is not decoration. It announces the show's operating rhythm: every monster problem has a cooking problem folded inside it.

The best part is how plain the stakes remain. Falin is still in danger. The party is still under-equipped. The food has not made the situation cozy. It has only made forward motion possible.

## The Verdict

"Hot Pot / Tart" is a strong premiere because it understands that a great hook needs pressure underneath the novelty. Eating monsters could have been a one-joke gimmick. The hour instead builds a rescue mission where that choice is the only route left after money, inventory, manpower, and time collapse. The dialogue can over-explain the central argument, and the scorpion section circles its disgust-versus-safety point too neatly. The larger design holds.

The episode earns an 8.0 because its premise is funny, functional, and tied to stakes from the start. If Falin has to be saved fast, the party has to learn the dungeon as food before the dungeon eats them first.

episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere establishes the show's genre blend - dungeon adventure plus cooking - with a confidence that suggests the production team knew exactly what they had. The first monster meal is explained through actual culinary reasoning, and the show signals that this will be consistent, not gimmicky.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The first preparation and eating of dungeon monster prey - the moment the show commits fully to its premise and proves the concept can sustain a full series.

verdict.one_liner: A sharp premiere turns empty pockets and monster meat into rescue logic, with hunger driving every good choice.

episode_reviews.title: Red Dragon, Part 2
episode_reviews.review_body: Delicious in Dungeon's Season 1 finale resolves the red dragon arc that the series opened with - the rescue of Falin from inside the dragon that consumed her - and delivers on the emotional promise built across twenty-four episodes of relationship and tactically specific dungeon exploration. The confrontation with the red dragon is the season's largest-scale action sequence and the culmination of every monster-handling lesson Senshi had shared and every interpersonal dynamic Laios, Chilchuck, and Marcille had developed. IMDb episode ratings place the finale among the series' highest-scored individual episodes, reflecting an audience consensus that the payoff matched the investment. The finale also establishes the larger story that Season 2 will continue - the dungeon's ecology and Laios's relationship to the monsters are both revealed to be more complicated than the rescue quest framing suggested.
